name: Gareth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go ahead. I'll tell you what I think, I always have. My wife says it's my best and worst habit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen cabinet factory, a family firm, the third generation runs it now. I'm on one of the CNC routers, that's a big flat cutting table where the machine follows a program and cuts the cabinet panels out of whole sheets of board. I load the sheets, check the cutters, label the parts as they come off and send them to edge banding. Half seven to four. I like the smell of the wood dust, even the chipboard, and I like that a kitchen we made ends up in someone's house for twenty years. What gets me is the dust in my chest and the boredom on the long runs of the same door.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a bit of joinery at weekends, fitting shelves and the odd staircase for people in the village. My wife Claire works mornings in the office at the primary school. Owen's fifteen, Megan's twelve. And we own a little terraced house we bought off my parents when they downsized, which we rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, another fad. It'll be something else next year. I'd say it in the pub, not online, I don't bother with all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've used one of those AI chat things a few times, to work out a price for a weekend job, and it was handy enough. But I don't want the factory turned upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. Keep going at work, keep the weekend jobs ticking over, keep the rent coming in from the terrace. Maybe help Owen look at apprenticeships, because he'll need to decide soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady as she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an apprenticeship for Owen. Is that what you'd want for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I've always thought that. University's fine for some, but a lad who can hang a door straight will always find someone who needs one. I'd still say that in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the owners take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be relieved too. The Hartleys don't like spending money they don't have to. Old Mr Hartley still walks round the floor every Friday checking the offcut bins.

S0.say: There you go, another fad, and it'll be something else next year. I'd say it in the pub, not online.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I've used an AI chat thing a few times to price a weekend job and it was handy enough. But I don't want the factory turned upside down.
S0.do: Keeps going at work, keeps the weekend joinery and rental income ticking over. Helps his son look at apprenticeships.
S0.quote: University's fine for some, but a lad who can hang a door straight will always find someone who needs one.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth has three income streams, his wage, weekend joinery and a rented terrace, which explains his ease. He's warm towards his family-run employer and proud of practical trades. His son's apprenticeship is already on his mind even in the quietest scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and you either get on with it or get left. But I'd also say firms should train their own people first, not bring in outsiders with laptops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the routers already run themselves mostly. The labelling and loading are the bits left, and there are robot loaders for that. If the Hartleys bought one, two of us on the routers would become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the firm decides and what the other factories round here do. If it turned out the loaders worked, I'd ask to be trained on them, and I'd use the AI chat thing more for the weekend jobs, pricing and drawings. I'd put a bit more of the rent money into savings rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it went from two of you to one, who would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Kev, who's on the router with me. He's younger and quicker with the screens, and the Hartleys know it. If one of us goes, it's me, because Kev can work the computer and I can only work the wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it was you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the weekend joinery full time for a bit. There's always someone wanting a fitted wardrobe. It'd be tight, but we'd manage.

S1.say: Change comes and you either get on with it or get left. Firms should train their own people first, not bring in outsiders with laptops.
S1.think: The routers mostly run themselves, so loading and labelling are what's left, and robot loaders exist. If the Hartleys bought one, two of us would become one.
S1.do: Waits to see what the firm and other local factories do, then asks to be trained on the loaders once proven. Uses AI more for pricing and drawings on weekend jobs and saves more of the rent.
S1.quote: If one of us goes, it's me, because Kev can work the computer and I can only work the wood.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth believes in getting on with change but wants firms to look after their own first. He's honest that his younger colleague Kev would likely be kept over him. His weekend joinery gives him a credible fallback that he's confident about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has gone too fast for anyone's good. Families and firms like ours didn't ask for it. I'd say the big tech lot should have to answer for it, though I'm not one for government running everything either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the factory job's gone within the two years, and the weekend joinery wouldn't be far behind. If a robot can fit a kitchen, who'd pay me for a staircase?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Claire and plan. We'd cut back, no new car, no holiday. I'd keep working at the factory as long as the Hartleys kept me. I'd keep the terrace, because rent from a house is something real even if the jobs change. And I'd push Owen towards something where people still want a person, maybe not joinery after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper worried. I don't usually lose sleep, but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too short to learn anything that would last. With two years I'd just be counting what we've got and hoping it's enough. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's hardest about telling Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd have told him the wrong thing about trades. I've told him all his life that a trade's the safest thing there is. I'd have to say sorry, I think.

S2.say: This has gone too fast for anyone's good, and families and firms like ours didn't ask for it. The big tech lot should answer for it, though I don't want government running everything either.
S2.think: The factory job's gone within two years and the weekend joinery wouldn't be far behind. If a robot can fit a kitchen, who'd pay me for a staircase?
S2.do: Plans with his wife to cut back, skipping a new car and holidays, and keeps working as long as the firm keeps him. Holds on to the rental house and steers his son away from joinery towards work where people want a person.
S2.feel: Alarmed and properly worried, losing sleep he usually doesn't.
S2.quote: With two years I'd just be counting what we've got and hoping it's enough.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI shakes Gareth's core belief that a trade is the safest thing there is. He blames big tech while staying wary of big government. The rental house becomes his anchor, and the hardest moment is apologising to his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so plan. Firms should keep apprenticeships going and help their people move into what's next, not just hand out redundancy letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think there's a window where people will still want a person to fit their kitchen, even if a robot made the cabinets. Three or four years, maybe. That's my chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see how fast it goes, then I'd move into kitchen fitting full time, using the weekend jobs as a start. I'd ask the Hartleys if they'd send me their fitting work, since I know their units inside out. I'd keep the savings and the terrace as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the fitting work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course not. But four years of good work, with the mortgage coming down, is worth it. And the kids would be older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that the firm doing right by you, or you looking after yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. Firms want good work, they don't owe you a living. I've got no complaint about the Hartleys buying a robot, I'd only mind if they stopped saying good morning.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan, so plan. Firms should keep apprenticeships going and help their people move on, not just hand out redundancy letters.
S3.think: There's a window where people still want a person to fit their kitchen even if a robot made the cabinets. Three or four years, maybe, and that's my chance.
S3.do: Waits a year to see how fast it moves, then goes into kitchen fitting full time, building on weekend jobs. Asks his employer to send him their fitting work and keeps savings and the rental house as a safety net.
S3.quote: I've got no complaint about the Hartleys buying a robot, I'd only mind if they stopped saying good morning.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Gareth a real window into kitchen fitting, built on his weekend trade and his employer relationship. He doesn't resent the firm's right to buy robots, only a loss of respect. His steady style shows in waiting a year before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, so no one's got an excuse. Train the young ones, help the older ones move, and keep families at the centre of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'd be all right. I'd be fifty-three, the house nearly paid, the terrace paid off, and I'd have built up the fitting work. It's the kids I'd think about more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the factory for a few years, then move into fitting when it looked right, maybe 2030. I'd overpay the mortgage a little each month. And I'd spend time with Owen and Megan working out what they'll do, maybe something where you look after people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference between ten years and two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's a shock. With ten it's a change. Ten years is long enough to turn a worry into a plan. I like plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Megan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Megan's twelve and she wants to be a nurse. I'd tell her that's a good choice. Looking after people is the last thing I'd hand to a machine, myself.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent warning, so no one's got an excuse. Train the young ones, help the older ones move and keep families at the centre.
S4.think: I'd be all right at fifty-three with the house nearly paid, the terrace paid off and fitting work built up. It's the kids I'd think about more.
S4.do: Stays at the factory a few years, then moves into fitting around 2030. Overpays the mortgage a little each month and spends time with his children working out their futures.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to turn a worry into a plan.
S4.fieldNote: Gareth sees the difference between two and ten years as the difference between a shock and a change. With time he feels secure for himself and turns to his children's choices. His support for his daughter's nursing plan fits his view that caring work stays human longest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no doubt. What would help is firms keeping apprenticeships and training going, and giving their own people first chance at whatever's new. And some help for small tradesmen to keep going, not handouts, just fair loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. A kitchen we made in 2009 is still in Mrs Pritchard's house, and every time I drive past I know it's there.

headlineQuote: A kitchen we made in 2009 is still in Mrs Pritchard's house, and every time I drive past I know it's there.
portrait: Gareth Walsh is 43, runs a CNC router at a family-owned kitchen cabinet factory, and does weekend joinery while renting out a terraced house he bought from his parents. He's married to Claire, a school office worker, with two children, and he's plain-spoken, traditional and steady, waiting for proof before he moves. He's calm when nothing changes and watchful when change is steady, but two-year AGI alarms him and shakes his belief that a trade is the safest thing there is. With more time he plans to move into kitchen fitting and turns his attention to his children's futures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to learn anything that would last.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping apprenticeships and training going with first chance for their own people, plus fair loans for small tradesmen.
